Strategist: Over two dozen 'serious people' exploring 2028 White House bid

More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.

Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.

"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.

He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.

He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.

Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"

Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.

"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.

"It's going be the most interesting presidential [election] since 2008."

Four midterms takeaways for 2028 White House race

What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

Messina, who went on to become Obama's deputy chief of staff at the White House, said the party's success in the US midterm elections was down to their ability to stay focused on the economy and the effect of Donald Trump's tariffs, which were "devastating to rural voters".

"When you're a farmer and you're paying $7 for a gallon of diesel to put in your tractor, the economics just don't work, and at the same time you're paying more for everything," he said.

PODCAST: Hear more from Jim Messina on Americast

Staying on message about the economy helped them flip seats in traditionally strong Republican states like Iowa, Kansas, and Texas, he said.

"The common criticism of Democrats is that we can't stick to one message. And for the first time in a very long time, Democrats stuck to the economy. They didn't take the bait on the social wars," he said.

Messina cautioned Democrats that success in this year's midterm elections was not a ringing endorsement of the party and that "the MVP of the election for the Democrats was Donald Trump".

The hard part will now be bringing the party's progressive and centrist wings together in Congress, he said.

Watch: 'I was surprised to be confronted and spoken to in that way,' Sunday Times journalist says

Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".

"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.

She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.

In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".

On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.

The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."

Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

Ian Winter, pictured here in 2014, reported himself to the regulator

On Thursday, he was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week trial.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Channel 4 Dispatches, Sunday Times and Times programme.

Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.

Brand is also being investigated over two more rape allegations made by two other women.

Court documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court, held before Brand's criminal trial, suggest one of the women was 16 at the time of the alleged offence and appeared in a Channel 4 documentary. Brand has denied the allegations.

Brand faced further questioning from officers in July 2025

On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.

He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand .

Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry.

Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.

At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."

In January 2026, wildfires in Chile caused the evacuation of more than 50,000 people

Many extreme weather events are becoming more common and more intense around the world, fuelled by human activities such as the burning of fossil fuels.

Here are four ways that rising temperatures are affecting weather extremes.

Even a small increase in average temperatures makes a big difference to heat extremes.

As the range of daily temperatures shifts to warmer levels, hotter days become more likely and more intense.

Scientists use computer models to simulate how individual extreme weather events unfold in two scenarios:

today's world with about 1.4C , external of human-caused warming

a hypothetical world without human influence on the climate

That way, they can estimate , external how much a particular heatwave, storm or drought was affected by climate change.

The UK experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.

Five widespread heatwaves affected the country, resulting in 40 days of temperatures above 30C (86F).

Head of Climate Attribution at the Met Office, Dr Mark McCarthy, described summer 2026 as "remarkable" and warned that extreme heat events would only become more common as the world warms.

What is net zero and is the UK on track to achieve it?

Climate change has also intensified multiple heatwaves across the world this year, according to scientists at the World Weather Attribution group (WWA).

Examples include Australia's worst heatwave in six years in January, the 45C that India experienced in April and Europe's deadly June temperatures .

Heatwaves can happen as a result of heat domes , external , which are created when an area of high pressure stays over the same area for days or weeks, trapping hot air underneath.

Higher temperatures in the Arctic - which has warmed nearly four times faster than the global average , external - may be affecting the fast band of winds high in the atmosphere known as the jet stream.

One theory suggests that this is making heat domes more likely, although this is not clear cut.

For every 1C rise in air temperature, the atmosphere can hold about 7% more moisture , external .

With more moisture available, rainfall can become heavier.

UK winters were 13% wetter , external in the decade from 2016 to 2025 than between 1961 and 1990, the Met Office says.

However, the large annual variation in rainfall makes it difficult to draw conclusions from a single decade, its scientists warn.

Globally, heavy rainfall events have become more frequent and intense over most land regions due to human activity, according to the UN's climate body, the IPCC , external .

For example, in October 2025, Hurricane Melissa became one of the strongest hurricanes to ever hit the Caribbean.

WWA researchers found that climate change increased extreme rainfall associated with the storm by 16%.

A drought in Puerto Rico led to water rationing in summer 2026

Linking climate change with specific droughts can be difficult because there are lots of different factors that affect the availability of water.

Natural weather systems like El Niño can play a key role, as was the case with drought in southern Africa in early 2024 .

But climate change is shifting global rainfall patterns. While some of the world is getting wetter, other parts are becoming drier, which can make them more prone to drought.

And heatwaves fuelled by climate change can worsen dry conditions when they do occur by increasing evaporation from the soil.

This makes the air above warm up more quickly, leading to more intense heat.

During periods of hot weather, increased demand for water, especially from farmers, puts even more stress on the water supply.

Severe drought declared and hosepipe bans in force - is your area affected?

Climate-driven heatwaves worsened drought conditions throughout Europe this summer, according to the EU's Joint Research Centre , external .

Four of Europe's key rivers - the Loire, Po, Rhine and Danube - reached record low levels .

Drought was declared in all of Wales and two-thirds of England, with the highest category - "severe drought" - being used for the first time in parts of southern England.

Elsewhere, the WWA found that climate change intensified a severe drought in Jamaica and Puerto Rico from May 2026.

Global warming made extreme dry conditions 40% more likely , external in Jamaica and 30% more likely in Puerto Rico, the WWA said.

Fires happen naturally in many parts of the world.

It is difficult to know if climate change has caused or worsened a specific wildfire because other factors are also relevant, such as changes to the way land is used.

But climate change is making the weather conditions needed for wildfires to spread more likely, the IPCC says , external .

Extreme, long-lasting heat draws more moisture out of soils and vegetation.

These tinder-dry conditions provide fuel for fires, which can spread at incredible speeds, particularly if winds are strong.

In January 2026, fires in Chile and Argentina resulted in 55,000 evacuations. The area burned was around 36% larger due to climate change, according to a global report on wildfires , external .

More than 5,000 wildfires burned across Canada this summer, resulting in some of the worst air quality levels in the world being recorded in nearby cities.

Climate change made the conditions which enabled the fires to spread twice as likely, according to the WWA , external .

Wildfires produced record air pollution in Canadian cities this summer

Many fires are started deliberately or accidentally by humans. But rising temperatures may also increase the likelihood of lightning in some forests, which can in turn trigger more fires.

The combined effects of shifting land use and climate change mean extreme wildfires are projected to become more frequent and intense globally, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) , external .

The number of the most extreme fires may rise by up to 50% by 2100, UNEP suggests.

2026 was the UK's second worst year for wildfires after 2022, according to provisional data , external from the housing department.

In Stourbridge, two fires destroyed 19 homes on the hottest day of the year.

'It’s not always the case that people know everything about people in public life,' says Burnham on Brand

The head of the Metropolitan Police said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about entertainer and comedian Russell Brand.

On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault .

Met Police boss Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

Brand was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday.

Speaking to the BBC, Sir Mark said that he "wouldn't be surprised if more people came forward" about Brand and said there were "two ongoing rape investigations" into him.

Brand has already been interviewed under caution in relation to those allegations.

Sir Mark praised the bravery of the women who came forward to tell their story to the police and during the trial.

"That's a real challenge for anyone having gone through something so ghastly and you have to admire them."

The head of the Met also said that whilst Brand's case "may look different because it's about celebrity, the majority of sex offending is about people abusing power", adding that victims will be believed.

"We will do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful person who is responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life," he said.

Watch: Met Police releases Brand interview footage

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also spoken about the case, seeking to explain the Labour Party's previous association with Brand, saying "it's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life".

Some within the party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

Now foreign secretary, Miliband has since said he regrets the interview . The BBC has approached Miliband for comment.

In 2014, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted in support of Brand on Twitter following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned with.

In his 2014 tweet, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham told the BBC : "His crimes are horrific".

"All I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do."

Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court

It was put to Sir Mark during an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme that Brand's defence barrister "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark said that what he heard reported from the trial was "very close to victim blaming".

Asked whether he would support the Victim's Commissioner's call for a legal duty in the Courts and Tribunals Bill that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

He said he would "strongly support" such a decision, adding: "It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case."

Brand was refused bail following his conviction on Thursday and will now spend the weekend in custody before a return to court on Monday for sentencing.

He is expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

Once the trial was over, it was reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme .

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.

Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.

Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Bayles and another member of Brand's staff had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did.

Shortly after, he sexually assaulted her.

She had complained to her manager, who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.

In recent years, Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.

In a statement, Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.

"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."

Bayles said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".

He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

Bayles said this was why he decided to stop working with Brand in 2010 and had not had any contact with him since. He added that during his time with Brand, no complaints were made about the entertainer's behaviour.

"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events

Human activities are causing world temperatures to rise, posing serious threats to people and nature.

Things are likely to worsen in the coming decades, but scientists argue urgent action can still limit the worst effects of climate change.

Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.

The world has been rapidly warming for around a century, causing weather patterns to change.

Since the 1980s, each decade has been warmer than the previous one, the Met Office says.

2024 was Earth's hottest year on record , with climate change mainly responsible for the high temperatures.

It was also the first calendar year to surpass 1.5C of warming compared to "pre-industrial" levels of the late 1800s, according to the Copernicus climate service , external .

Temperatures remained high in 2025 , despite a slight cooling from a natural weather pattern called La Niña.

The opposite El Niño pattern , combined with climate change, makes it likely that 2026 will also rank among the hottest years ever recorded.

The climate has changed naturally throughout the Earth's history.

But natural causes cannot explain the particularly rapid warming seen over the last century, according to the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

This has been without doubt caused by human activities, especially the widespread use of fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - in homes, factories and transport systems.

When fossil fuels burn, they release greenhouse gases - mostly carbon dioxide (CO2). This CO2 acts like a blanket, trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface. This causes the planet to heat up.

Since the start of the Industrial Revolution - when humans began burning large amounts of fossil fuels - the level of CO2 in the atmosphere has risen by more than 50% .

The CO2 released from burning fossil fuels , external has a distinctive chemical fingerprint. This matches the type of CO2 increasingly found in the atmosphere.

Climate change has already had a huge effect, including:

more frequent and intense extreme weather , such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall

rapid melting of glaciers and ice sheets, contributing to sea-level rises

warmer oceans , which can fuel more intense storms and harm sea life

These changes are already having serious consequences for people and economies around the world.

In August 2026, the partial collapse of a glacier caused an avalanche of ice and rock to descend on Nepal and Tibet

Flash floods in Nepal killed more than 1,400 people in August 2026. Nepal's Finance Minister, Swarnim Wagle, said it could cost up to a tenth of the economy to rebuild.

Climate change increased the chances of the glacier collapse which triggered the flood, World Weather Attribution group scientists said.

The more the world warms, the worse the impacts of climate change become.

Nearly 200 countries pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in the 2015 Paris agreement .

That target is generally understood to mean an average annual increase of 1.5C over 20 years rather than a one-off rise in a single year.

Long-term warming of 1.5C would bring serious consequences for many populations.

But an increase of 2C or more would bring even greater impacts, the IPCC says.

increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather

greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue

more species being threatened with extinction

The call to restrict temperature rise to 1.5C was partly designed to avoid crossing so-called "tipping points".

It is not clear exactly where they sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.

These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet , warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest .

The Earth's poles are especially vulnerable to rising temperatures

About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people are highly vulnerable to climate change, the IPCC says.

People living in poorer countries are expected to suffer most as they have fewer resources to adapt.

This has led to questions about fairness , external , because these places have typically only been responsible for a small percentage of greenhouse gas emissions.

However, knock-on impacts could be felt over wide areas. For example, crop failures linked to extreme weather could raise food prices globally.

Reaching net zero CO2 emissions is essential to limit global warming, the IPCC says.

This means reducing emissions as much as possible and actively removing any remaining emissions from the atmosphere.

Most countries have, or are considering, net zero targets , external .

There has been encouraging progress in some areas, such as renewable energy and electric vehicles.

But humanity's CO2 emissions are still at record highs , causing long-term warming to reach 1.4C in 2025.

The latest UN Emissions Gap Report , external said the 1.5C limit was likely to be breached in the coming years.

A return to 1.5C by 2100 was possible, but it would require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the report added.

Otherwise, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the UN said.

World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments.

In 2025, the COP30 climate conference ended without any new agreements on fossil fuels or deforestation in the final deal.

Countries had previously agreed on the need to "transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems" at the COP28 talks in 2023.

At COP29 in 2024, richer countries committed to giving developing nations at least $300bn (£223bn) a year by 2035 to help them tackle climate change. But this is far less than poorer countries say they need.

Governments are gathering in Turkey for the next round of talks, COP31 , in November 2026.

Major changes need to come from governments and businesses, but individuals can help through actions like:

improving their home's insulation and energy efficiency

switching to electric vehicles or living car-free

replacing gas boilers with electric systems like heat pumps

MN202611_7ivul9s0u3.t:
Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from a fund for damages linked to climate change after flash floods in August 2026

In Paris in 2015, almost 200 countries signed a landmark agreement designed to limit global warming to 1.5C and avoid its worst impacts.

But despite some progress in areas like renewable energy, the world has continued to warm at a rapid pace.

A recent UN report said the target was likely to be breached in the next few years and that "urgent and stringent" action would be needed to return the world to 1.5C.

The Paris Agreement is at the heart of the international commitment to tackle rising global temperatures.

It came into force on 4 November 2016 and saw almost all the nations of the world agree to cut the greenhouse gas emissions which cause global warming.

However, the United States - the world's second biggest greenhouse gas emitter - withdrew from the deal in January 2026 under President Donald Trump.

The US also withdrew during Trump's first presidency, but it rejoined in 2021 under his successor President Joe Biden.

The only other UN member states outside the Paris agreement are Iran, Libya and Yemen.

The Paris Agreement lists a series of commitments:

to "pursue efforts" to limit global temperature rises to 1.5C, and to keep them "well below" 2.0C above those recorded in pre-industrial times, generally considered to mean the late 19th Century

to achieve a balance - known as net zero - between the greenhouse gases that humans put into the atmosphere and the gases that they actively remove, in the second half of this century

each country to set its own emission-reduction targets, reviewed every five years to raise ambitions

richer countries to help poorer nations by providing funding, known as climate finance, to adapt to climate change and switch to renewable energy

The 1.5C target is generally accepted to refer to a 20-year average rather than a single year.

So, while 2024 was more than 1.5C warmer than pre-industrial times , it did not mean the Paris Agreement threshold has been breached

Every 0.1C of warming brings with it greater risks for the planet, such as longer heatwaves, more intense storms and wildfires, according to climate scientists .

But a very large body of scientific evidence shows that warming of 2C or more would bring far greater impacts, on top of those felt at 1.5C, UN scientists say.

more people being exposed to extreme heat

higher sea levels as glaciers and ice sheets melt

increased risks to food security in some regions due to more extreme weather

greater chances of some climate-sensitive diseases spreading, such as dengue

more species being threatened with extinction

Some changes could become irreversible if so-called "tipping points" are crossed.

It is not clear exactly where these sit, but once these thresholds are passed, changes could accelerate and become irreversible.

These could include the collapse of the Greenland Ice Sheet , warm Atlantic Ocean currents or further loss of the Amazon rainforest .

How climate change worsens heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floods

The Paris deal restated a 2009 commitment that richer countries should provide $100bn (£73bn) annually by 2020 to help developing nations deal with the effects of climate change and build greener economies.

Although only $83.3bn was raised in 2020, data from the OECD , external shows the goal was reached in each of the three years after 2022.

Almost two-thirds of the money in recent years has gone towards efforts to limit global warming, while around a quarter has been used to help nations adapt to climate change.

In 2023, countries agreed for the first time that a fund should be established exclusively for loss and damage . This is money to help countries recover from the impacts of climate change.

Nepal became the first country approved to receive money from the fund after a flash flood in August 2026 killed more than 1,400 people.

At COP29 in 2024, richer nations committed to providing $300bn (£219bn) a year to developing nations by 2035. Developing countries - which had hoped for more - criticised the "paltry sum".

World leaders meet every year to discuss their climate commitments at international summits known as COPs (Conference of the Parties).

All COPs since 2015 have tracked how countries are building on what they promised in Paris.

At COP28 in 2023 , countries agreed for the first time to "contribute" to "transitioning away from fossil fuels", although they were not forced to take any specific action.

Countries also agreed to treble the global capacity of renewables - such as wind and solar - by 2030.

But the final deal at COP30 in 2025 failed to directly mention fossil fuels. Instead, the host of the conference, Brazil, published a voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels, which will be discussed at COP31.

That COP is taking place from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Turkey and is co-hosted by Australia .

A "coalition of the willing" composed of 57 countries has also organised its own conferences separate from the COP process to discuss phasing out fossil fuels.

The first meeting was held in Santa Marta, Colombia in April 2026, and another conference is scheduled for July 2027 in Tuvalu.

The long-term 1.5C global warming target has not yet been breached.

But the latest UN Emissions Gap Report , external said the limit was likely to be exceeded in the next few years after "decades of insufficient climate action".

In the "lowest possible" scenario, warming would still reach 1.7 to 1.8C by the mid-century, the report said.

A return to 1.5C by 2100 is possible, but it will require "urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions", the UN added.

Specifically, emissions would need to be cut by 18% between 2025 and 2030.

The report found that the pledges governments have made so far would only cover half of these cuts.

Without further action, global warming could reach nearly 3C by the end of the century, the research said.

Cole Palmer last represented England in March

Thomas Tuchel's brutal assessment of Cole Palmer's exclusion from England's latest squad made it crystal clear Chelsea's gifted playmaker faces a fight to save his international career under the German head coach.

"He misses too many opportunities to impress" was Tuchel's blunt explanation for Palmer's absence, after the 24-year-old withdrew the previous England camp citing a minor injury.

Tuchel's message was so stark, so pointed, that Palmer must now be wondering when he will get another opportunity to impress.

And, to make it even more chastening, Tuchel took his decision after receiving assurances that Palmer was fully fit and available for selection for England's upcoming Nations League games - at home to Croatia then against World Cup holders Spain in Madrid.

There is believed to be surprise from inside Palmer's camp that he has not been included, but Tuchel has proved in the past there is no sentiment or star system in operation on his England watch.

Palmer's fall from grace with England can be illustrated by the fact he was regarded as part of a golden future when he scored a superb goal in a losing cause against Spain in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin.

He was a contentious omission from England's squad for the World Cup last summer, but Tuchel's selection was shaped at that point by Palmer's indifferent season at club level with Chelsea - along with injury problems.

This latest setback encapsulates an England career that has been stop-start since making his debut under Tuchel's predecessor, Sir Gareth Southgate, in a 2-0 win against Malta in a European Championship qualifier at Wembley in November 2023.

He has won 14 England caps, with two goals and one assist, his last appearance coming in the number 10 role in the disappointing 1-0 defeat by Japan at Wembley in March, when he was substituted after less than an hour.

More tellingly, perhaps, is that he has only figured in three of Tuchel's 26 games since he succeeded Southgate.

Far from being a centrepiece of England's plans, Palmer is now on the outside looking in, with seemingly no immediate prospect of forcing his way back.

'Palmer misses too many opportunities to impress' - Tuchel

Palmer was offered reassuring words of sorts by Tuchel, but his predicament is now clear. He has allowed others to form an orderly queue in front of him in England's pecking order. They are now Tuchel's priority, not Palmer.

Tuchel said: "We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp, because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together.

"I guess everyone is desperate to play with England and Cole is the same. He misses too many opportunities to impress. It was a long camp but the players in that camp brought something extraordinary."

"It's not personal. We will never assume Cole is in the mindset never to come to the camp, but we stick to the guys who were in camp last time. It was excellent. The impact of all the players was immense. We have Josh King as a new player, who can play as a 10 and on both wings."

He added: "Cole is always in our mindset but the competition is on."

There may be additional pain, and perhaps a measure of puzzlement, for Palmer in that Tuchel has not just decided to stick with the players from the last camp - calling up Fulham's King and, the major incoming surprise, 21-year-old Jobe Bellingham from Borussia Dortmund.

Palmer said he had played for Chelsea with "discomfort and pain" before the last round of England fixtures, which included a 3-2 loss to Spain at Wembley, a win away to the Czech Republic, a Wembley victory in that return fixture and a 7-0 rout of Croatia in Rijeka.

And Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has also insisted Palmer was "struggling" in Chelsea's 3-0 defeat at Brentford before the international break.

It is believed Palmer's desire to play for England remains as strong as ever, with the fact that his state of fitness was checked out before Tuchel named his squad taken as a sign he remains in his thoughts.

Alonso confirmed England had made checks on Palmer, adding: "When a player is fully fit he is selectable. When he is not fit we give the national team the reasonable information to decide together. Sometimes it's not good for the player."

Chelsea's boss said he has not spoken to Palmer about his England exclusion and has no doubts about his character, although the pair had talks about his recent sending off in the 2-0 home loss to Tottenham Hotspur.

He said: "We have not talked about England. We are focused on Chelsea things, how to help him, how he can become more and more influential. These are our topics to talk.

"We speak about Chelsea. We have enough on our plate. My impact area is my control area and what we talk about.

"I am very happy with his quality, with his attitude and the impact he is having with the rest of the team."

Even before Palmer withdrew last time out, Tuchel had previously said he had a "point to prove" and needed "to step up" to "keep his shirt and justify the nomination".

Is Tuchel convinced Palmer has the motivation to play for England? Does his "trust" lie elsewhere?

He certainly has options in the position Palmer would occupy, with Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham his world class "number 10" and another Chelsea player, Morgan Rogers, an outstanding alternative.

Morgan Gibbs-White, Eberechi Eze and now 19-year-old King, who has won his first England senior call-up, have been selected ahead of Palmer, with Everton's Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall also given a glowing reference from Tuchel, despite not making the squad.

Alonso praises Palmer's quality and attitude

Palmer has made a good start to the season with Chelsea. The penalty he scored in the 2-0 win against Manchester United was his 50th league goal for the club in only 105 games.

This, however, has cut no ice with Tuchel, who has not just relegated him down the list of players included in England's squad, but out of his plans completely for now.

Tuchel has never been shy of taking hard-nosed decisions without a backward glance, such as excluding Jude Bellingham from England's squad for games against Latvia and Wales in October 2025, despite the player's insistence he was keen to be involved after recovering from shoulder surgery.

Achieving "net zero" is the world's key strategy to fight climate change, which is already having serious consequences for people and nature around the globe.

But the political consensus around the UK's net zero policies has collapsed, with the Conservative and Reform parties now branding them too difficult and expensive.

Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.

Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.

Greenhouse gases include carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane. Their levels in the atmosphere are increasing rapidly due to human activities, including burning fossil fuels, chopping down forests and farming.

In practice, reducing these emissions means switching from coal, oil and gas to cleaner energy sources like wind and solar power.

It also involves adopting green technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps to replace petrol or diesel cars and gas boilers.

But not all emissions can be eliminated.

So remaining emissions must be matched by things like planting trees, restoring peatlands or using machines to remove CO2 from the air.

But there are limits to these "carbon removal" techniques in scale and cost. That is why most of the focus is on drastically reducing emissions in the first place.

The world is warming because of humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, which increase global temperatures by trapping extra energy in the atmosphere near the Earth's surface.

This is bringing more heatwaves and extreme weather as well as melting ice sheets and raising sea levels .

In 2026, the UK experienced its hottest summer on record , which the Met Office said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.

Aiming to avoid the worst of these impacts, nearly 200 countries signed the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement. A target was set to reach net zero globally in the second half of the century.

Around 140 countries , external have their own net zero targets, covering roughly three-quarters of global emissions and 80% of the world's population.

It's widely accepted that richer nations will need to get to net zero before poorer ones, which often have fewer resources to switch to cleaner technologies and have contributed less to climate change historically.

Sea-level rises increase the chances of coastal flooding during storms

The UK's greenhouse gas emissions have fallen sharply: in 2025 they were 54% lower than in 1990, according to provisional data , external .

This figure only includes emissions generated within the UK and not from products manufactured abroad and imported.

Successive UK governments have pledged to reach net zero by 2050 and the target was written into law in 2019.

To help achieve this, the current Labour government has committed to:

rapidly increase wind and solar generation to achieve "clean power" by 2030

end the sale of new fully petrol and diesel cars by 2030

subsidise electric heat pumps to replace gas boilers

invest in technology to capture and store CO2

What is the Paris agreement and why does 1.5C matter?

These policies began to be implemented under Sir Keir Starmer's government and have continued to be pursued by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

However, recent decisions have led some environmentalists to question whether the government can still meet its targets:

Approving the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea

Reducing planned investment in heat pumps and carbon capture , external to pay for defence

Holding a consultation on whether to weaken electric car targets

The chancellor's support for a third runway at Heathrow

In June, the government's independent adviser, the Climate Change Committee (CCC), warned that the UK was "not moving fast enough" , external towards net zero.

However, the Chancellor, John Healey, said in his autumn budget speech , external that the government remained "unshakably committed" to the goal.

Heat pump installations are rising but remain below targets

When former Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May signed the UK's 2050 net zero target into law in 2019, it passed through parliament with the support of all major parties.

But that political consensus has since fragmented. The term "net zero" is often used by critics to attack environmental targets, which they claim are being put ahead of economic goals.

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is "determined" to meet the 2050 deadline, a policy also backed by the Liberal Democrats.

Meanwhile, the Green Party wants net zero "as soon as possible, and more than a decade ahead of 2050".

These parties argue that it's in the UK's economic interest to move away from fossil fuels, which can be volatile in price. Supplies can also be interrupted by international events like the US-Israel war on Iran .

But the Conservatives and Reform UK want to scrap the UK's net zero target, calling the current plans costly and unachievable.

They argue that, in isolation, the UK's efforts make little difference to climate change, not least because UK emissions are much smaller than those of countries like China and the US.

The SNP has targeted net zero by 2045 for Scotland, while Plaid Cymru has introduced a 2040 deadline in Wales.

There is no single path to net zero, which means there is no fixed price.

But the Climate Change Committee says the policy will require tens of billions of pounds a year by the end of the 2020s, most of which it expects to come from the private sector rather than government spending.

By the early 2040s, the CCC calculates that the savings from moving away from fossil fuels to cleaner, more efficient technologies should outweigh the costs , external .

Multiple studies have found that, globally, the economic cost of tackling climate change is much smaller than letting warming continue unchecked, which would result in widespread and increasing climate hazards.

However, as with any transition, the costs and benefits can be unequally felt. For example, while there is huge potential for new clean energy jobs, those employed in the oil and gas industry are likely to be negatively affected.

More fake bomb threats disrupt flights across Europe

With no fewer than 32 bomb threats affecting a dozen airlines in the space of four days, the aviation industry is facing another potential crisis.

Some of the threats apparently came from phone calls, others via email, and although they have all turned out to be hoaxes, they were each clearly serious enough to force emergency action.

Some planes had to be escorted by military jets, others were quietly inspected mid-air by cabin crew - desperate not to cause alarm.

A number had to be re-routed from their original destinations, landing at different airports, sometimes in different countries. An Aer Lingus flight had to land at an airbase 1,000 kilometers from its intended destination after running low on fuel.

New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines

All this poses a serious challenge to the airlines, who have little idea who is causing the severe disruption they have faced almost every day this week.

Although so far all threats have turned out to be hoaxes, airlines have no choice but take each threat seriously.

"They have a triage system, but follow the same protocols for each until they are absolutely sure there is no threat," says Marco Chan, a former commercial airline pilot and aviation expert at Kingston University.

"That could involve a mid-air inspection, but definitely a search once the plane has landed.

"Passengers might not even know there is an issue until they are told to disembark. It can cause disruption, but that is a small price to pay when safety is at stake", he adds.

The sight of sniffer dogs and specialist teams on the tarmac searching for explosives on commercial planes may cause alarm.

So far, the disruption too has been limited to the few thousand passengers who have been directly involved.

Paul Mason, an aviation security expert, says there will be a financial cost to the airline involved, but planes get diverted every day.

"The number can sometimes run to over a hundred planes daily, for things like technical issues, medical emergencies, even the weather," he adds. "They far outweigh the few which have been diverted due to hoaxes. So airlines are well equipped at dealing with the unexpected."

It is also unlikely that customers will be able to get refunds, he explains, because these incidents are not the fault of the airlines.

The more worrying aspect over the past few days will be the seeming random nature of the targets and the lack of any credible intelligence regarding who is behind the threats.

Aside from emails suggesting that an extremist misogynist group had claimed responsibility for a handful of the incidents - although since denied by its founder - there appear to be few leads.

With 20 years of military experience as well, Paul Mason says the incidents bear the hallmarks of hybrid warfare, which involves unconventional methods such as cyber attacks.

"It does feel co-ordinated," he says. "Russia has said it's got nothing to do with it, but it could be proxies. It's a very easy way to create disruption and chaos, with plausible deniability."

"That's the problem. Someone can have an opinion on who is behind it, but if the perpetrators are using sophisticated technology, it will be very hard to trace them."

He does say however that if misguided individuals try to copy the threats they could find themselves in serious trouble.

The Aviation Security Act 1982 states that "intentionally communicating false, misleading, or deceptive information that endangers - or is likely to endanger - the safety of an aircraft in flight is a serious criminal offence".

The maximum sentence is life imprisonment.

There is precious little that airports and airlines can do to guard against actually receiving threats, as they can come from a vast range of sources. But the punishment is designed to act as a deterrent.

As Paul Mason warns: "Someone might think it's a laugh and very easy to do, but unless they are very sophisticated, they are highly likely to be traced. And find themselves facing prison."

U Rwanda na Isirayeli byiyemeje gukomeza kwagura ubufatanye mu guteza imbere inganda ndangamuco zishingiye ku ikoranabuhanga, hagamijwe kongerera ubushobozi abahanzi, kubafasha kwihangira imirimo no kubyaza umusaruro ibihangano byabo.

Ibi byagarutsweho ku wa 5 Ugushyingo 2026, ubwo hasozwaga icyumweru cyahariwe guteza imbere inganda ndangamuco n’ikoranabuhanga, cyateguwe mu rwego rwo gushimangira ubufatanye bw’ibihugu byombi.

Muri iki cyumweru, abahanzi n’ibigo umunani byo mu Rwanda bahawe amahugurwa agamije kubongerera ubumenyi mu guhanga udushya, kwihangira imirimo hifashishijwe ikoranabuhanga no kumenya amahirwe ari mu nganda ndangamuco zishingiye ku ikoranabuhanga, zizwi nka Creative Industries.

Nyuma y’amahugurwa, abitabiriye iki gikorwa bamuritse imishinga yabo, basobanura uruhare ishobora kugira mu guteza imbere sosiyete no guteza imbere urwego rw’ubuhanzi.

Mu mishinga yamuritswe, itatu yahize indi yahembwe amafaranga arimo ibihumbi 5.000 by’amadolari ku mwanya wa mbere, ibihumbi 3.000 ku wa kabiri n’ibihumbi 2.000 ku wa gatatu.

Veda Muvunyi wo mu Mujyi wa Kigali yavuze ko yishimiye kuba umushinga we na bagenzi be ujyanye n’umuziki waratoranyijwe mu yahize indi, ashimangira ko inkunga bahawe izabafasha kuwagura no kongera ibikorwa byabo.

Ati: “Aya mafaranga agiye kudufasha kongera ibikorwa byacu no gufasha abahanzi benshi bo mu Rwanda kujya babona amafaranga aturuka ku bihangano byabo.”

Umunyamabanga Uhoraho muri Minisiteri y’Urubyiruko n’Ubuhanzi, Parfait Ishungure, yavuze ko ubu bufatanye bugaragaza ko umubano w’u Rwanda na Isirayeli utagarukira gusa mu bya dipolomasi, ahubwo unagera no mu zindi nzego zirimo ubuhanzi n’ikoranabuhanga.

Yasobanuye ko abahanzi n’abandi bakora mu nganda ndangamuco bahawe amahugurwa n’inkunga bazabifashisha mu kongera ubushobozi bwabo, guteza imbere urwo rwego no kuzamura abahanzi, ari na bo bagenerwabikorwa ba nyuma.

Ati: “Ni no kugira ngo nk’igihugu, tubashe guha urubyiruko rwinshi, cyane cyane abakora ibihangano n’ibikorwa bitandukanye ku mbuga nkoranyambaga (content creators), akazi, bityo bagire uruhare mu iterambere ry’igihugu muri rusange.”

Ambasaderi wa Isirayeli mu Rwanda, Einat Weiss, yavuze ko igihugu cye kizakomeza gushyigikira urubyiruko rw’Abanyarwanda mu rwego rwo kubafasha guteza imbere impano zabo no kwagura imishinga yabo.

Ati: “U Rwanda ni igihugu gifite ubushobozi budasanzwe n’urubyiruko rwinshi rufite impano. Abazagera ku ntego zabo bazabera abandi urugero rwiza.”

Yavuze ko bifuza gukomeza iyi gahunda no mu mwaka utaha, kugira ngo bazasuzume umusaruro izaba yaratanze.

Minisiteri y’Urubyiruko n’Ubuhanzi, ku bufatanye na Minisiteri y’Ikoranabuhanga na Inovasiyo, Urugaga rw’Abikorera mu Ikoranabuhanga (ICT Chamber) na Ambasade ya Isirayeli mu Rwanda, ivuga ko izakomeza gushyigikira ibikorwa byo kongerera ubumenyi abahanzi n’abandi bakora mu nganda ndangamuco.

Ubu bufatanye bugamije kubafasha kunoza ibyo bakora, gukoresha ikoranabuhanga mu guhanga no kumenyekanisha ibihangano byabo, ndetse no kubibyaza umusaruro ubateza imbere.

Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and Republican Vice-President JD Vance

Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways. Here are four takeaways.

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.

While he has previously said he has no plans to run for president, his successful campaign, with several viral moments, helped boost his national profile.

Another potential Democratic nominee, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro , swept aside his Republican challenger.

Shapiro has not committed to a 2028 run but analysts point to his broad appeal in swing-state Pennsylvania as a sign that he could be competitive on the national stage.

Illinois Governor JB Pritzker also won after a campaign pundits in his state described as a "tune-up" for a presidential run.

California Governor Gavin Newsom could not run for re-election in the midterms but he is invested in the outcome of a ballot initiative to tax the state's wealthy residents which he campaigned against.

On the Republican side, there were two potential 2028 names running in Arkansas.

Republican Senator Tom Cotton and Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders - a one-time Trump administration press secretary - were able to stay in office by a narrower margin than before, both earning just above half of the votes in the conservative state.

Trump names Stephen Miller as new chief of staff

What Democrats can and can't do with their new power after taking Congress

Exit polls suggest the swing against Republicans was partly due to anger felt by voters at the actions of the Trump administration.

That could present a challenge to his potential successors who come from the ranks of the current leadership, including Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio .

"The one person who has been hurt badly by this election campaign is Vance," said Karen Beckwith, a professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio.

Vance has already sought to distance himself from defeat - and from a foreign policy adventure in Iran that was politically disastrous for his party.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote on X.

Rubio has denied reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.

Other possible Republican candidates may benefit from not being part of the administration. Some have been staking out a position on what went wrong and what next.

In a lengthy post on X, Senator Ted Cruz , who was not running this year, said that too many Republican politicians seem like "they didn't care" about the economic issues faced by voters.

"It is dark right now, but it is always darkest before the dawn, and morning is coming," he wrote. "That is my fervent prayer, and that is my commitment to you."

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis , who abandoned his 2024 presidential run after being trounced by Trump early on, was similarly critical and pointed to Republican victories in Florida as a sign of what can be accomplished.

Former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie was blunt in his assessment: "The Trump era is over."

White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war

Both the centrist and left wings of the Democratic Party have claimed victory from the results as each side sifts through possible 2028 contenders.

Dozens are already making moves, Obama's former adviser Jim Messina has told the BBC.

El-Sayed's win in Michigan was a breakthrough moment for left-wing Democrats because he triumphed in a swing state.

His supporters now claim his win could supercharge left-wing candidates in the 2028 election.

"The old notions of electability are out the door, and bold economist populist outsiders proved they can win in battleground states," said Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

Green added that the "water is now warm" for candidates such as New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run in presidential primaries and "know that they can win."

Moderate Democrats, however, claimed victories across the country, with the "Blue Dog Caucus" of moderate and conservative Democrats gaining at least 14 seats in Congress, nearly doubling its current size.

This has led many within that wing of the party to conclude that centrist candidates that bill themselves as pragmatic and willing to work with conservatives could woo Republican voters.

Given the success of Democratic candidates who focused on cost of living issues, an economy-first approach will likely be a focus again in two years.

Amirah Siquierah, the director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, said successful candidates in 2028 will combine economic populism with newer concerns such as data centres.

Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide

Both parties must contend with a changing political map and a shifting coalition of support for 2028.

Once "safe" Republican parts of the country can no longer be considered conservative strongholds.

Texas is left with only one Republican at a statewide level, which means its 40 electoral college votes could be up for grabs in 2028.

Christina Pascucci, a political commentator and one-time Senate candidate in California, said the midterms "challenge long-held political assumptions" and show that "neither party can afford to take its traditional strongholds for granted".

That is true of both Democrats and Republicans who will need to win over swing voters, added Pascucci, now the CEO of Atlas Impact, a global communications and advisory firm.

"Neither party owns these voters," she said.

Texas has a new Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa

The Trump coalition of working class and Latino voters faltered, reversing many of the gains he had made with those electorates in his successful 2024 campaign.

Driena Sixto, a former spokesperson for Turning Point USA and a conservative political commentator, told the BBC that she believed that Republicans will have to change their messaging to Latino voters ahead of 2028 for any future candidate to be able to reverse the trend.

"Last time, the campaign message was one of safe communities and fighting back against trafficking," she said.

"After the president was sworn in, I think a lot of messaging from the White House did too much to highlight deportations. That was the divide."

French gendarmes and rescue workers at the scene of the crash in Lent, eastern France

A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.

The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.

The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.

French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families.

In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.

The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".

The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.

The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".

The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood.

Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.

Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.

"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."

Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".

Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."

Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".

Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot (centre) arrived at the scene following the crash

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the accident was tragic, and thanked the firefighters, medical teams and police who attended the scene.

Earlier, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".

Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.

More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.

The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

Watch: Protesters demonstrate against Trump’s proposed arch

A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.

Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.

Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.

The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.

"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.

It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.

The White House criticised the federal court that temporarily halted construction as an "activist district court."

"We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch," the spokesperson said.

An artist's rendering of Trump's proposed arch near Arlington Cemetery

A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

A website that the White House shared on social media on Friday also shows a video rendering of the arch that shows the structure emblazoned with the words "Golden Age of America" along one side.

It refers to the structure as "The Military Triumphal Arch".

The proposed structure is sprinkled with appliques that are visually similar to the golden embellishments Trump has added to the Oval Office.

The Trump administration has also said the arch would double as a complex to store military equipment - complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones.

"There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump previously wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that out of "the 59 top cities and Capitals", Washington is "the only one in the world that does not have a triumphal arch". He did not specify to which cities he was referring.

Mark Paoletta, the chairman of the NCPC and one of the Trump appointees, said at Thursday's meeting that the president understood "it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments".

How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image

He and other commissioners said the structure fulfils a 100-year plan to build a monumental work on Columbia Island, just as Congress and various commissions intended.

Paoletta added that the arch would honour the nation, its veterans and "provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves".

Anne Wright is among those who are opposed to the arch

Anne Wright, who spent 29 years in the US military and also worked in the diplomatic service, told the BBC she would try to stop the construction.

"We'll tie ourselves to the bulldozer, we've got veterans in wheelchairs and we'll chain the wheelchairs to these things," she said.

Wright referenced this week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party lost control of Congress, saying: "[Trump's] policy of war, of ego – they've been rejected."

Fellow veteran John Pomeroy - who served in the Air Force for six years, including during the Vietnam War, and whose parents are buried at Arlington - said the arch "would lessen the solemn nature of a visit to the cemetery".

He described Trump's suggestion that the arch could store military equipment as "silly" and a "half-baked idea", arguing it would be a target for terrorist attacks.

Like Wright, Pomeroy said he would "impede construction workers as much as I can" if they came to the site to begin work.

Trump signs order preventing future presidents from changing Oval Office

Democratic Congressman Jared Huffman argued in his statement to the commission that the arch would disrupt sightlines not just of Arlington but of the Lincoln Memorial, fracturing "a view meant to underscore the unity and sacrifice of the American people, and doing that with a structure we often associate with emperors or kings who built grand arches as tributes to themselves".

"This is a tribute to Donald Trump," Huffman added.

Lawsuits have been filed against the plans, raising concerns about the environment, traffic congestion and safety. There is also a disagreement over whether congressional approval is needed to build the arch.

It is one of several construction projects Trump has proposed for the US capital. That includes at the White House, where he is facing legal challenges over the construction of a ballroom, which is estimated to cost $400m (£300m).

His plans to renovate a 106-year-old golf course, which he has dubbed "trash island", is also being challenged in the courts.

European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.

On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.

It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ , evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.

The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week , in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".

Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats

A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.

France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.

No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.

As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.

Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.

In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".

Armed gardaí were deployed to RTÉ'S Dublin headquarter after a bomb threat

While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".

In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.

"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.

Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.

Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.

Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.

The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".

"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."

Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings .

Queens Alik, Flesh, Naya Thorn and Mocha made it to the final episode

Warning: This article includes spoilers for the finale of RuPaul's Drag Race UK.

After 10 weeks of toe-to-toe lip-syncs, fierce runways and shady remarks, the time has come for one queen to be named the UK's next Drag Race superstar.

For the final time on the BBC, 12 contestants were whittled down to just one after the broadcaster announced it was axing RuPaul's Drag Race UK due to budget cuts.

On Thursday night, RuPaul crowned Flesh as the series eight winner.

The London queen snatched the title from Mocha, Naya Thorn and Alik, who also made it to the final episode.

The 26-year-old was crowned by last year's winner, Bones, who is also her best friend and drag sister, with the duo performing together as Heavenly Bodies.

Speaking to BBC Newsbeat after celebrating overnight, the Soho queen says the win still feels "surreal" and she spent the whole evening "smiling, crying, and laughing".

She will be the last queen crowned on the BBC before the UK edition moves to Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

While some fans have welcomed the prospect of a new chapter for the series which might include bigger cash prizes, like in other spin-offs, others fear leaving the BBC will mean less representation for LGBTQ+ culture.

Flesh says the move to Wow could widen the range of performers and subcultures featured on the show, but worries the shift to subscription could reduce the audience for drag.

"This is where it feels slightly sadder that we're leaving the BBC because for all of the parameters that it created that limited what we could do, there was more exposure than drag has ever been given," she says.

She admits she is "concerned" about the "knock-on effect" this could have on the future of the UK drag industry, such as creating fewer opportunities for contestants.

"Without that exposure, there will be less demand and with less demand and less exposure, events won't be able to be created," she says.

Flesh was crowned by last year's winner, and her drag sister, Bones

Amid this concern, Flesh encourages people to connect with their local drag community and performers to consider ways they can evolve performances to bring in new audiences.

The decision to shelve the programme was announced shortly after the latest series began airing , with the BBC saying it was facing "very difficult choices" amid "significant financial pressures".

Flesh was awarded the £25,000 cash prize after impressing the judges in the final maxi challenge, which saw the last four queens perform a megamix of girl group anthems from past series.

Wrapping the show's stint on the BBC this way felt like a "really fun and tasteful way to reflect on the iconography of Drag Race UK", says Flesh, who hopes the past contestants feel "honoured".

But she reveals the final group of queens did think the "writing was on the wall" for show's future when they were asked to do the mix.

Flesh has stood out across the series as a fashion queen, bringing looks to the runway that RuPaul said would go down in the series' history.

Speaking to RuPaul and judge Michelle Visage during the final episode, Flesh said Drag Race "tells people it's not only OK to be them but it's a gift and a dream, and to be crowned the UK's next drag race superstar would be mine coming true".

She made it through the series without ever being in the bottom two and only had to lip-sync for the first time in the final when the top three queens battled it out for the win.

After Alik was eliminated, Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn performed a rendition of David Bowie's Modern Love.

Final three Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn lipsynced to David Bowie's Modern Love after Alik was eliminated

It wasn't only the UK's next Drag Race superstar recognised by RuPaul during the finale episode - the Miss Congeniality title is typically awarded to the friendliest and kindest queen.

This year that title was awarded to Paris Baby, who created more than her fair share of drama across the series, in particular her spats with Staffordshire queen KY Kelly.

Miss Congeniality is decided by a secret cast vote and the queens were visibly shocked when RuPaul said Paris had won by a landslide.

At the start of the series, Paris said she had been blocked on social media by some of her competitors, including Flesh, but said they were now "besties".

"Hopefully the world can now see there's a lot more to Paris Baby," she said.
